frames.narration: t=0. Alice logs in with password and MFA. The auth server will issue an RS256 access JWT valid 5 minutes and a refresh token r1.
The auth server signs the JWT with its private key (kid k1, exp = t+5 min) and returns it with r1. Services fetch the matching public key from the JWKS endpoint once and cache it.

t=1 min. Alice calls Orders with Authorization: Bearer <JWT>. Orders pins RS256, finds kid k1 in its cached JWKS, verifies the signature, then checks exp, iss and aud. Zero lookups, no call to the auth server.
The same token also works at Billing (its aud lists both services), again with no call to the auth server. This is why JWTs fit many microservices: no shared session store on the hot path.

t=2 min. A script injected into the page reads localStorage and sends the JWT and r1 to an attacker. The attacker calls Orders and is accepted: the signature is valid, so Orders cannot tell it is not Alice.
t=3 min. Alice's app refreshes: r1 is exchanged for a new JWT and r2, and r1 is marked used (refresh rotation). The stolen JWT is unaffected and still expires at t=5 min.

t=4 min. The attacker presents r1 to the auth server. It was already used, so this is reuse: the server revokes the whole family (r1, r2). The attacker gets 401, Alice must log in again, and the stolen JWT still works for one more minute.

t=5 min. The stolen JWT passes its exp. Orders rejects it with 401, so the exposure after the theft was 3 minutes. A 24 hour token would have given the thief 23 hours 58 minutes, and a server-side session would have stopped working the moment its key was deleted.
